en: Majjhima Nikāya 96:
The Discourse to Esukārī.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the brahmin Esukārī approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Esukārī said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe four kinds of service:
they prescribe service for a brahmin, they prescribe service for a kshatriya, they prescribe service for a vaishya, and they prescribe service for a shudra.
In this regard, Master Gotama, this is how the brahmins prescribe service for a brahmin:”
‘A brahmin should attend upon a brahmin, or a kshatriya should attend upon a brahmin, or a vaisya should attend upon a brahmin, or a sudra should attend upon a brahmin.
This, Master Gotama, is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a brahmin.
And here, Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a kshatriya:
‘A khattiya might serve a khattiya, a vessa might serve a khattiya, or a sudda might serve a khattiya.
This, Master Gotama, is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a khattiya.
And here, Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a vessa:
‘A vaiśya should serve a vaiśya, or a śūdra should serve a vaiśya.
This, Master Gotama, is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a vaiśya. Now, Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a śūdra:
‘Only a śūdra should serve a śūdra.
Who else indeed would serve a śūdra?
This, Master Gotama, is what the brahmins prescribe as service for a śūdra.
“Brahmins, Master Gotama, prescribe these four kinds of service.
What does the venerable Gotama say about this?
“But, brahmin, has the entire world authorized the brahmins to prescribe these four kinds of service?”
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.

“Suppose, brahmin, there were a man who was poor, destitute, and indigent. While he was unwilling, they might force a hook into his mouth, saying: ‘Good man, you must eat this meat, and you must pay for it.
In the same way, brahmin, the brahmins prescribe these four modes of service without the consent of those ascetics and brahmins.”
“Brahmin, I do not say that everything should be served; nor do I say, Brahmin, that nothing should be served.
For if, Brahmin, by serving someone for the sake of service one becomes worse and not better, I do not say that such a person should be served.
But if, Brahmin, by serving someone for the sake of service one becomes better and not worse, I say that such a person should be served.”
And if they were to ask a kṣatriya thus, brahmin:

“Between one who, by serving you, would become worse rather than better because of that service, and one who, by serving you, would become better rather than worse because of that service—whom would you serve here?
then a kṣatriya, brahmin, answering correctly, would answer thus:

‘For if, while serving someone, because of that service I were to become worse and not better, I would not serve them; but if, while serving someone, because of that service I were to become better and not worse, then I would serve them.
Whether it be a brahmin, O brahmin, or even a merchant, O brahmin... [and so on].
“Furthermore, brahmin, if they were to ask a *sudda* thus:
‘Between that which is worse for you because of serving it, rather than better, and that which is better for you because of serving it, rather than worse— which of these would you serve?’—
then a *sudda*, brahmin, answering correctly, would answer thus:”

‘For if, while serving someone, because of that service I were to become worse and not better, I would not serve them; but if, while serving someone, because of that service I were to become better and not worse, then I would serve them.
Brahmin, I do not say that being born into a high family is better, nor do I say that being born into a high family is worse.
Brahmin, I do not say that having a magnificent appearance is better, nor do I say that having a magnificent appearance is worse.
“Brahmin, I do not say that great wealth is better, nor do I say, Brahmin, that great wealth is worse.
For even one born here into a high family may be a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one of wrong conduct in sensual pleasures,
a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a speaker of idle chatter, and full of covetousness.”
He is ill-willed, he has a mind of malice, and he holds wrong view.
Therefore, I say that high birth is not the best.
For even one of high birth here, O Brahmin, may abstain from taking life and abstain from taking what is not given.
He abstains from sexual misconduct; he abstains from false speech; he abstains from malicious speech;
he abstains from harsh speech; he abstains from idle chatter; he is free from covetousness;
he is of a mind without ill will; and he holds right view.
Therefore, I say that high birth does not make one worse.
For even one of noble appearance, brahmin... [and so on]... [as before].
For even one who possesses abundant wealth, brahmin, may here be a destroyer of life...
[and so on] ...may hold wrong view.
Therefore, I say that "being of great wealth is not better.
For even one who is of great wealth here, O Brahmin, may abstain from taking life... [and so on] ...and possess right view.
Therefore, I say that "being of great wealth is not worse."
“Brahmin, I do not say that everything should be served; nor do I say, Brahmin, that nothing should be served.
For whatever service, Brahmin, when being performed, causes faith to increase, virtue to increase, learning to increase, generosity to increase, and wisdom to increase—that, I say, should be served.
But whatever service, Brahmin, when being performed, does not cause faith to increase, nor virtue to increase...”
“His learning does not increase, his generosity does not increase, and his wisdom does not increase; I do not say that such a person is one who should be attended upon.
When this was said, the brahmin Esukārī addressed the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe four kinds of wealth:”
They prescribe wealth for a brahmin, they prescribe wealth for a kshatriya, they prescribe wealth for a vaisya, and they prescribe wealth for a sudra.
In this regard, Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe alms-gathering as the wealth of a brahmin;
yet a brahmin who holds alms-gathering in contempt becomes a doer of what ought not to be done, like a cowherd taking what is not given.
"Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a brahmin.
And here, Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe the bow and quiver as the wealth of a kshatriya;
for a kshatriya who holds the bow and quiver in contempt becomes a doer of what ought not to be done, like a cowherd taking what is not given."
“Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a kshatriya.
And here, Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a vassala: agriculture and cattle-tending.
Yet, Master Gotama, a vassala who looks down upon his own wealth—agriculture and cattle-tending—becomes a doer of what should not be done, like a cowherd who takes what has not been given.”
"Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a merchant.
And here, Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a worker: the sickle for reaping.
Yet a worker who holds the sickle in contempt as his wealth becomes a doer of what ought not to be done, like a cowherd taking what has not been given."
“Master Gotama, this is what the brahmins prescribe as the wealth of a sudra.
Master Gotama, these are the four kinds of wealth that the brahmins prescribe.
What does Master Gotama say about this?”
“But, brahmin, does the entire world authorize the brahmins, saying: ‘Let them prescribe these four kinds of wealth’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.

“Suppose, brahmin, there were a man who was poor, destitute, and indigent. While he was unwilling, they would force a hook into his mouth, saying: ‘Good man, you must eat this meat, and you must pay for it.’”
"In the same way, brahmin, the brahmins, without the consent of those ascetics and brahmins, nevertheless proclaim these four kinds of wealth.
But I, brahmin, proclaim the noble, supramundane Dhamma as the true wealth of a person.
For one who recollects his ancient maternal and paternal lineage, wherever the manifestation of his individual existence occurs, by that alone he is reckoned."
If the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a kṣatriya family, one is reckoned as a "kṣatriya";
if the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a brahmin family, one is reckoned as a "brahmin";
if the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a vaiśya family, one is reckoned as a "vaiśya."

If the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a family of sudras, it is reckoned simply as a “sudra. Just as, brahmin, whatever fuel a fire burns in dependence upon, by that alone it is reckoned: if a fire burns in dependence on wood, it is reckoned as a “wood-fire”; if it burns in dependence on grass, it is reckoned as a “grass-fire”; if it burns in dependence on cow-dung, it is reckoned as a “cow-dung-fire”; if it burns in dependence on chaff, it is reckoned as a “chaff-fire”; if it burns in dependence on rubbish, it is reckoned as a “rubbish-fire. So too, brahmin, if the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a family of khattiyas... in a family of brahmins... in a family of vessas... in a family of sudras, it is reckoned simply as a “sudra. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. If one performs a deed of a khattiya, one is reckoned as a khattiya; if one performs a deed of a brahmin, one is reckoned as a brahmin; if one performs a deed of a vessa, one is reckoned as a vessa; if one performs a deed of a sudra, one is reckoned as a sudra. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. If one performs a deed of a khattiya, one is reckoned as a khattiya; if one performs a deed of a brahmin, one is reckoned as a brahmin; if one performs a deed of a vessa, one is reckoned as a vessa; if one performs a deed of a sudra, one is reckoned as a sudra. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. If one performs a deed of a khattiya, one is reckoned as a khattiya; if one performs a deed of a brahmin, one is reckoned as a brahmin; if one performs a deed of a vessa, one is reckoned as a vessa; if one performs a deed of a sudra, one is reckoned as a sudra. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. If one performs a deed of a khattiya, one is reckoned as a khattiya; if one performs a deed of a brahmin, one is reckoned as a brahmin; if one performs a deed of a vessa, one is reckoned as a vessa; if one performs a deed of a sudra, one is reckoned as a sudra. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. For this reason, brahmin, it is not fitting for you to say: “The khattiya is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior; the brahmin is the highest caste, the other castes are inferior. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin, one is reckoned by the deed one performs. If one performs a deed of a khattiya, one is reckoned as a khattiya; if one performs a deed of a brahmin, one is reckoned as a brahmin; if one performs a deed of a vessa, one is reckoned as a vessa; if one performs a deed of a sudra, one is reckoned as a sudra. It is not fitting for you to speak thus. Why is that? Because here, brahmin,
If a fire burns dependent on wood chips, it is reckoned as a "wood-chip fire";
if a fire burns dependent on grass, it is reckoned as a "grass fire";
if a fire burns dependent on cow dung, it is reckoned as a "cow-dung fire."
In the same way, brahmin, I prescribe the noble, supramundane Dhamma as a person’s wealth.
When one recollects one’s ancient maternal and paternal lineage, wherever the manifestation of one’s personal existence occurs, by that alone one is reckoned.
If the manifestation of one’s personal existence occurs in a khattiya family, one is reckoned simply as a “khattiya.”
If the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a brahmin family, one is reckoned simply as a "brahmin";
if the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a merchant family, one is reckoned simply as a "merchant";
if the manifestation of a personal existence occurs in a laborer family, one is reckoned simply as a "laborer."
Brahmin, even if one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a khattiya family,
and having relied upon the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from unchastity, abstains from false speech, and abstains from malicious speech, from harsh speech...
He abstains from speech, he abstains from idle chatter, he is free from covetousness, he has a mind without ill will, and he holds right view;
he is one who attains the noble, wholesome Dhamma.
And if, brahmin, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness from a brahmin family, he [attains] what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
Relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya, he abstains from taking life... [and so forth] ...he possesses right view;
he is one who succeeds in the methodical, wholesome Dhamma.
Even if, Brahmin, he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a merchant family, and he [practices] what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
Relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya, he abstains from taking life... [and so forth] ...he possesses right view; he is one who attains the method, the Dhamma that is wholesome.
Even if, Brahmin, he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a family of low birth, yet he [is one who has realized] what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya, one abstains from taking life... [and so forth] ...one possesses right view;
one is a successful achiever of the methodical, wholesome Dhamma.
What do you think, brahmin?
“Is it only a brahmin who is capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity and free from ill will—in this place, and not a khattiya, nor a vessa, nor a suddha?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.
For a khattiya too, Master Gotama, is capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity and free from ill will—in this place.”
For even a brahmin, Master Gotama...
for even a vaiśya, Master Gotama...
for even a śūdra, Master Gotama...
"For indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes are capable of developing a mind of loving-kindness—free from enmity and free from ill will—in this place.

"Even so, brahmin, if one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness from a khattiya family, having relied upon the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...up to right view."
He becomes one who attains the noble, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Whether from a brahmin family, brahmin,
or even from a vessa family, brahmin...
Brahmin, even if one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a clan of householders,
if— by relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata— he abstains from taking life … [and so on] … and possesses right view, he is a successful attainer of the method,
the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
“What do you think, brahmin?
Is it only a brahmin who is capable of taking a bath-robe, going to a river, and washing away dust and dirt, and not a khattiya, nor a vessa, nor a sudda?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
For even a khattiya, Master Gotama, is capable of taking perfumed soap, going to a river, and washing away dust and dirt;
so too, Master Gotama, is a brahmin...
and so too, Master Gotama, is a vessa...
"For even a *sudda*, Master Gotama...
indeed, Master Gotama, all four castes are capable of taking perfumes and unguents, going to a river, and washing away dust and dirt.
"In the same way, brahmin, if one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness comes from a khattiya family..."
And by resorting to the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, one abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...one possesses right view;
such a person is a successful attainer of the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
Whether it be from a brahmin family, O Brahmin...

If, brahmin, one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness—even from a clan of merchants or even from a clan of laborers—and having relied upon the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he possesses right view; he is a successful practitioner.
The noble Dhamma is wholesome.
What do you think, brahmin?
Suppose here a head-anointed khattiya king were to assemble a hundred men of various births:

‘Let those gentlemen who are born there into khattiya families, brahmin families, or royal families come, taking fire-drills made of śāka wood, or sāla wood, or salaḷa wood, or sandalwood, or padumaka wood, and produce fire; let them manifest heat.
But let those gentlemen who are born there into caṇḍāla families, nesāda families, veṇa families, rathakāra families, or pukkusa families come.’
“Could they, by taking a fire-drill from a dog trough, a pig trough, a washerman’s trough,
or from a castor-oil wood, produce fire and manifest heat?
“What do you think, brahmin?”

Now, suppose fire were produced and its heat manifested by taking a lower fire-drill from a kshatriya family, a brahmin family, or a royal family, using as kindling wood from a *sāka*, *sāla*, *salaḷa*, sandalwood, or *padumaka* tree—
would that fire indeed possess flames, color, and radiance, and would it be [effective] by that?
It is possible to perform the function of fire by means of fire; however,
that fire which is produced by taking an upper fire-drill from a caṇḍāla family, a hunter family, a bamboo-worker family, a cartwright family, or a scavenger family, or from a dog-skin basket,
a pig-skin basket, a dyer’s basket, or from castor-wood— [is it possible to perform the function of fire by means of that?]
“If one were to expose the heat of fire, would that fire not be without radiance, without color, and without luster,
and would it not be impossible to perform the functions of fire with such a fire?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
For even that fire, Master Gotama, which has been produced and kindled by means of a lower drilling stick made from the wood of a Khattiya family,
a Brahmin family, a royal family, or from the wood of the *sāka*, *sāla*, *salaḷa*, sandalwood, or *padumaka* tree—
that fire is indeed possessed of flames, beautiful in color, and radiant; and it is possible to perform work with that fire.
To perform the fire-making rite:

even that fire which is produced by taking an upper fire-stick from a dog trough, or a pig trough, or a washerman’s trough, or from castor-wood, by those born from outcaste families, hunter families, bamboo-worker families, cartwright families, or scavenger families.
“If fire were produced from heat, its flame would be radiant, beautiful, and bright, and it would be possible to perform the functions of fire with that fire.
For indeed, Master Gotama, every fire has a flame, is beautiful, and is bright, and it is possible to perform all the functions of fire with every fire.”

“In the same way, brahmin, even if one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a khattiya family relies on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and abstains from taking life … [and so on] … possesses right view,
he is a fulfiller of the true, wholesome Dhamma.”

Whether, O Brahmin, he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a brahmin family, or from a merchant family, or even from a laborer family, and he [practices] what has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
Relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya, he abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from unchastity, abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech,
abstains from idle chatter, is free from covetousness, and is of a mind without ill will.
“There is right view; one becomes an achiever of the true Dhamma that is wholesome.
When this was said, the brahmin Esukārī said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! … [as above] …”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The sixth discourse, the Esukārī Sutta, is finished.
